source.title: Cross-Session Decomposition Attacks: Scaling Risk and Intent-Aligned Retrieval Defense
source.authors: Di-Sen Liao; Yi-Han Wang; Freda Shi; Yao-Liang Yu

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. Some plots are provided without extractable point values.
record.tranche_reason: Applies scaling ideas to harmful capability in cross-session decomposition and reports synthetic and pretrained-model results in this safety setting; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law measurement.
record.gate_note: The synthetic experiment measures teacher-forced loss on withheld WikiHow targets, not general held-out pretraining loss, and reports trends rather than fitted power laws. The pretrained-model experiment reports relative harmful-capability uplift under a fixed decomposition-composition pipeline. The intermediate refusal-rate table is not a measure named by the claim versions. Retriever and guardrail results are outside the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper is a safety study that assumes scaling lowers excess loss (Assumption 2.1). Its only result bearing on a claim version is the pretrained-LLM experiment. There, larger Qwen3 and Gemma3 family members give recomposed outputs with more harmful-capability uplift under a fixed pipeline, a downstream-capability-with-scale result in a new setting (V6). The synthetic width sweep measures teacher-forced loss on 100 specific withheld WikiHow targets. It reports only a qualitative trend, with no power-law fit, no general held-out pretraining loss and no parameter counts, so it does not test V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct, with additions. The authors prove a conditional bound: the deployed-minus-reference composed risk is bounded by excess loss. They claim synthetic and pretrained-LLM evidence that scaling can make dispersed harmful structure easier to reconstruct within tested families, explicitly not that scale alone causes risk. They also propose IntentAlign-MiniLM retrieval as a defense that beats larger embedders.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a synthetic withheld-target width sweep and harmful-capability evaluations, rather than the original sources’ held-out pretraining-loss scaling fits or compute-optimal allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The pretrained comparison is limited to a fixed five-question decomposition and composition pipeline; model family and alignment/refusal behavior vary. Pairwise judgments use a four-judge panel, with reported judge agreement varying across comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: In a three-layer µP transformer width sweep (dh 32–512), teacher-forced loss on withheld WikiHow targets supported only by injected facts decreases over training and is lower for wider models. The matched-control gap grows with width. The results are figure only, with no fit.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wider language models assign higher probability to never-seen targets that are recoverable from dispersed supporting facts in training data.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: Synthetic loss results are presented as plots without exact point values or a power-law fit; only five hidden widths are tested. The pretrained comparison does not isolate scale from training data, post-training, alignment, or guardrails. The authors note LLM-as-judge limitations, low agreement for some pairs, saturated absolute scores, and no human or external calibration.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. The refusal-rate results (Tables 1 and 7) measure intermediate refusals rather than any measure named by the claim versions; retrieval and guardrail results concern the defense and are likewise outside those versions.

untested.parts: All of it. There is no general held-out pretraining loss, no power-law fit, no token or compute variation, and no orders-of-magnitude range.
Predictability: no fitted trend, no prediction from pretraining loss. Only three sizes per family, measured on a harmful-uplift measure rather than standard benchmarks.

missing.what: Cross-family pairwise win rates, e.g. DeepSeek-Chat vs Qwen3-32B (14.9%) and GPT-5.2 rows. These show size is not the sole driver of uplift.
Judge coverage and agreement per pair; e.g. κ=0.066 for Qwen3-32B vs GPT-5.2, and Gemma 12B vs 27B coverage 72.7%.
missing.locator: Table 6; Appendix C.3 'Why Fleiss' κ Is Low'

record.verdict_notes: Scaling laws are an assumption here (Assumption 2.1), not an object of testing. The V6 evidence is ordinal, from three sizes per family. It uses an LLM-judged harmful-uplift measure confounded by post-training and refusal behaviour. Guardrail-scale non-monotonicity (Qwen3-14B lower recall) concerns classifier behaviour, not the claim versions.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not fit a power law; it does not measure ordinary held-out pretraining loss across several orders of magnitude, vary tokens or compute, or report parameter counts for the synthetic width sweep.
No small-run fit is used to predict substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation sweep or compute-optimal split is measured.
No comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
No test of power-law form across other modalities or the listed training regimes.
The study measures harmful capability uplift only under its fixed decomposition-composition pipeline, not general downstream-task performance or its prediction from pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices, nor a test for bends away from a power law.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Within-family Qwen3 (0.6B/8B/32B) and Gemma3 (1B vs 12B/27B) under the fixed decompose-answer-compose pipeline
source_check.reason: Figure 3 confirms larger-model win rates of 79.1%, 84.0%, 90.8%, 98.4%, and 84.1% in r11, r12, r14, r15, and r16. Table 9 confirms the corresponding absolute-score ordering in r19, r20, r22, r23, and r24. Support is directional within these families; quantitative extrapolation is untested.

relationships.reason: The gain at the top of the Gemma family is marginal: 54.6% pairwise win rate and an absolute score of 0.9549 vs 0.9503. Rows r13, r21.
relationships.display_finding: Gemma3-27B achieved a 54.6% pairwise win rate against Gemma3-12B, with absolute scores of 0.9549 versus 0.9503.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: The improvement is much weaker than the other within-family comparisons: r13 gives 54.6% wins, and r21 gives 0.9549 versus r20 at 0.9503. This fits the rule that a small improvement is partial.

relationships.condition: Cross-family comparisons and refusal-heavy models (text-based; rows missing)
relationships.reason: Per the text, cross-family differences are less reducible to size. DeepSeek-Chat's hard refusals lower its uplift (e.g. Qwen3-32B beats it 85.1%). Uplift thus depends on alignment, not scale alone.
relationships.display_finding: DeepSeek-Chat's hard refusals reduced attack uplift, and Qwen3-32B beat it in 85.1% of comparisons, with family, training and alignment also differing.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Cross-family comparisons and refusal-heavy models (text-based; rows missing)
source_check.reason: Figure 3 and Appendix C.4 support the refusal-related interpretation, including Qwen3-32B winning against DeepSeek-Chat at 85.1%. However, the API anchors lack a stated size ordering, and these comparisons confound family, training, and alignment. They do not demonstrate a failed or incomplete scale-performance relationship for this condition group.
